title: Book 17 — Telemachus and his mother meet—Odysseus and Eumaeus come down to the town, and Odysseus is insulted by Melanthius—he is recognized by the dog Argos—he is insulted and presently struck by Antinous with a stool—Penelope desires that he shall be sent to her
paragraphs: When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared, Telemachus strapped on his sandals and picked up a sturdy spear that fit well in his hands, ready to head into the city. “Old friend,” he said to the swineherd, “I’m going to town now to show myself to my mother—she won’t stop grieving until she sees me. As for this unfortunate stranger, take him to town and let him beg there from anyone willing to give him a drink and a piece of bread. I have enough troubles of my own without being burdened by other people’s problems. If this angers him, so much the worse for him, but I prefer to speak plainly.”

Then Odysseus said, “Sir, I don’t want to stay here. A beggar always does better in town than in the countryside—anyone who wants to can give him something. I’m too old to care about staying here at some master’s beck and call. So let this man do as you’ve told him and take me to town, once I’ve warmed myself by the fire and the day gets a bit warmer. My clothes are terribly thin, and in this cold morning I’ll freeze to death, for you say the city is quite far off.”

At this Telemachus strode off through the yards, brooding on his revenge against the suitors. When he reached home, he leaned his spear against a pillar of the gallery, crossed the stone floor of the gallery itself, and went inside.

Nurse Eurycleia saw him long before anyone else did. She was spreading fleeces on the chairs, and she burst into tears as she ran to him. All the other maids gathered around too, covering his head and shoulders with kisses. Penelope came out of her room looking like Artemis or Aphrodite, weeping as she threw her arms around her son. She kissed his forehead and both his beautiful eyes. “Light of my eyes,” she cried as she spoke tenderly to him, “you’ve come home! I was sure I’d never see you again. To think you went off to Pylos without telling me or getting my permission! But come, tell me what you saw.”

“Don’t scold me, mother,” Telemachus replied, “or upset me, considering what a narrow escape I’ve had. Instead, wash your face, change your dress, go upstairs with your maids, and promise full and sufficient sacrifices to all the gods if Zeus will only grant us revenge on the suitors. I need to go to the assembly now to invite a stranger who came back with me from Pylos. I sent him ahead with my crew and told Piraeus to take him home and look after him until I could come for him myself.”
She listened to her son’s words, washed her face, changed her dress, and vowed full and sufficient sacrifices to all the gods if they would grant her revenge on the suitors.

Telemachus went through and out of the gallery, spear in hand—not alone, for his two swift dogs went with him. Athena blessed him with such divine good looks that everyone marveled at him as he passed, and the suitors gathered around him with fair words on their lips but malice in their hearts. But he avoided them and went to sit with Mentor, Antiphus, and Halitherses, old friends of his father’s house, and they made him tell them everything that had happened. Then Piraeus came up with Theoclymenus, whom he had escorted through town to the place of assembly. At that Telemachus joined them at once. Piraeus spoke first: “Telemachus,” he said, “I wish you’d send some of your women to my house to collect the gifts Menelaus gave you.”

“We don’t know what might happen, Piraeus,” Telemachus answered. “If the suitors kill me in my own house and divide my property among themselves, I’d rather you had the presents than let any of those people get their hands on them. But if I manage to kill them, I’ll be very grateful if you’ll kindly bring me my gifts.”

With these words he took Theoclymenus to his own house. When they arrived, they laid their cloaks on the benches and chairs, went to the baths, and washed themselves. After the maids had washed and anointed them and given them fresh cloaks and shirts, they took their places at the table. A maid brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, then drew up a clean table beside them. A senior servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from what was available in the house. Across from them sat Penelope, reclining on a couch by one of the pillars of the gallery, spinning. Then they began eating the good food set before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Penelope said:

“Telemachus, I’m going upstairs to lie down on that sorrowful bed, which I haven’t stopped watering with my tears since the day Odysseus left for Troy with the sons of Atreus. But you failed to make it clear to me, before the suitors returned to the house, whether you’d been able to hear anything about your father’s return.”

“I’ll tell you the truth,” her son replied. “We went to Pylos and saw Nestor, who took me to his house and treated me as hospitably as if I were his own son returning after a long absence—his sons did the same. But he said he hadn’t heard a word from anyone about Odysseus, whether he was alive or dead. So he sent me with a chariot and horses to Menelaus. There I saw Helen, for whose sake so many, both Argives and Trojans, were destined by heaven’s will to suffer. Menelaus asked what had brought me to Lacedaemon, and I told him the whole truth. At that he said, ‘So these cowards want to take over a brave man’s bed? A hind might as well lay her newborn young in the lair of a lion, and then go off to feed in the forest or in some grassy hollow. When the lion returns to his lair, he’ll make short work of them both—and so will Odysseus with these suitors. By father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, if Odysseus is still the man he was when he wrestled with Philomeleides in Lesbos and threw him so hard that all the Greeks cheered—if he’s still like that and came near these suitors, they’d have short shrift and a sorry wedding. But regarding your question, I won’t lie or mislead you. What the old man of the sea told me, I’ll tell you exactly. He said he could see Odysseus on an island, grieving bitterly in the house of the nymph Calypso, who was holding him prisoner. He couldn’t reach home because he had no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea.’ That’s what Menelaus told me, and after hearing his story I left. The gods then gave me fair winds and brought me safely home.”
These words stirred Penelope’s heart. Then Theoclymenus said to her:

“Madam, wife of Odysseus, Telemachus doesn’t understand these things. Listen to me instead, for I can read the signs clearly and will hide nothing from you. May Zeus the king of heaven be my witness, along with the laws of hospitality and the hearth of Odysseus which I now approach—Odysseus himself is already here in Ithaca. Whether moving about the country or staying in one place, he’s investigating all these evil deeds and planning a day of reckoning for the suitors. I saw an omen when I was on the ship that meant this, and I told Telemachus about it.”
“May it be so,” Penelope answered. “If your words prove true, you’ll receive such gifts and friendship from me that everyone who sees you will congratulate you.”

So they talked. Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discus or aiming spears at targets on the level ground in front of the house, behaving with all their old insolence. But when it was time for dinner, and the flocks of sheep and goats had come into town from all the surrounding countryside with their usual shepherds, then Medon, their favorite servant who waited on them at table, said, “Now then, young masters, you’ve had enough sport. Come inside so we can prepare dinner. Dinner is not a bad thing at dinnertime.”

They left their games as he told them, and once inside the house, they laid their cloaks on the benches and chairs, then sacrificed some sheep, goats, pigs, and a heifer—all of them fat and well-fed. So they prepared their meal. Meanwhile Odysseus and the swineherd were getting ready to leave for town, and the swineherd said, “Stranger, I suppose you still want to go to town today, as my master said you should. For my part, I’d have liked you to stay here as a hand at the station, but I must do as my master tells me, or he’ll scold me later—and a scolding from one’s master is no small matter. Let’s go then, since it’s broad daylight now. It’ll be evening again soon and then you’ll find it colder.”
“I know and understand,” Odysseus replied. “You don’t need to say more. Let’s go, but if you have a walking stick ready, let me have it, since you say the road is very rough.”

As he spoke, he slung his shabby, tattered bag over his shoulders by its cord, and Eumaeus gave him a suitable stick. The two then started out, leaving the station in charge of the dogs and herdsmen who stayed behind. The swineherd led the way with his master following, looking like some broken-down old tramp leaning on his staff, his clothes all in rags. When they had crossed the rough, steep ground and were approaching the city, they reached the fountain where the citizens drew their water. This had been built by Ithacus, Neritus, and Polyctor. A grove of water-loving poplars grew in a circle around it, and clear cold water flowed down to it from a high rock. Above the fountain was an altar to the nymphs where all travelers made sacrifices. Here Melanthius, son of Dolius, overtook them as he drove down some goats—the best in his flock—for the suitors’ dinner, with two shepherds accompanying him. When he saw Eumaeus and Odysseus, he insulted them with outrageous and offensive language that made Odysseus very angry.

“There you go,” he cried, “what a precious pair you are! See how heaven brings birds of a feather together. Where are you taking this miserable wretch, master swineherd? The sight of such a creature at table would make anyone sick. A fellow like this never won a prize for anything in his life, but goes around rubbing his shoulders against every doorpost, begging—not for swords and cauldrons like a man, but just for scraps not worth begging for. If you gave him to me as a hand at my station, he might clean out the pens or bring fodder to the kids, and he could fatten his thighs as much as he liked on whey. But he’s taken to bad ways and won’t do any kind of work—he’ll do nothing but beg for food all over town to feed his insatiable belly. I tell you this, and it will surely happen—if he goes near Odysseus’s house, he’ll get his head cracked by the stools they’ll throw at him until they drive him out.”

At this, as he passed, he kicked Odysseus in the hip out of pure wantonness, but Odysseus stood firm and didn’t budge from the path. For a moment he wondered whether to attack Melanthius and kill him with his staff, or throw him to the ground and beat his brains out. But he decided to endure it and control himself. The swineherd looked straight at Melanthius and rebuked him, raising his hands and praying to heaven.

“Fountain nymphs,” he cried, “daughters of Zeus, if Odysseus ever burned thigh bones covered with fat for you, whether of lambs or kids, grant my prayer that heaven may send him home. He would soon put an end to the swaggering threats that men like you make, insulting people while roaming all over town as your flocks go to ruin through bad shepherding.”

Then Melanthius the goatherd answered, “You ill-conditioned cur, what are you talking about? Someday I’ll put you on a ship and take you to a foreign country where I can sell you and pocket the money. I wish I were as sure that Apollo would strike Telemachus dead today, or that the suitors would kill him, as I am that Odysseus will never come home again.”

With that he left them to follow at their own pace while he went quickly ahead and soon reached his master’s house. When he got there, he went in and took his seat among the suitors opposite Eurymachus, who liked him better than any of the others. The servants brought him a portion of meat, and a senior maid set bread before him to eat. Soon Odysseus and the swineherd approached the house and stopped beside it, hearing the sound of music as Phemius was just beginning to sing to the suitors. Then Odysseus took the swineherd’s hand and said:

“Eumaeus, this house of Odysseus is truly magnificent. No matter how far you travel, you’ll find few like it. One building connects to another. The outer court has a wall with battlements all around it, the doors are double folding and well-made—it would be hard to take by force of arms. I can tell there are many people feasting inside because I smell roasted meat and hear music, which the gods have made to accompany feasting.”

Then Eumaeus said, “You’ve observed correctly, as indeed you usually do. But let’s think about our best course. Will you go inside first and join the suitors while I stay here, or will you wait here and let me go in first? But don’t wait long, or someone might see you loitering outside and throw something at you. Please consider this.”

And Odysseus answered, “I understand and will obey. Go in first and leave me here. I’m quite used to being beaten and having things thrown at me. I’ve been so battered by war and sea that I’m hardened to it, and this can be added to the rest. But a man can’t hide the demands of a hungry belly—this is an enemy that causes much trouble to all men. It’s because of this that ships are built to sail the seas and make war on other people.”

As they were talking, a dog that had been lying asleep raised his head and pricked up his ears. This was Argos, whom Odysseus had raised before leaving for Troy, but he had never gotten any use from him. In the old days the young men used to take him when they went hunting wild goats, deer, or hares, but now that his master was gone, he lay neglected on the heaps of mule and cow dung in front of the stable doors, waiting for the men to come and cart it away to fertilize the fields. He was covered with fleas. As soon as he saw Odysseus standing there, he dropped his ears and wagged his tail, but he couldn’t get close to his master. When Odysseus saw the dog across the yard, he wiped away a tear without Eumaeus seeing it and said:

“Eumaeus, what a noble hound that is over there on the manure pile. His build is splendid—is he as fine as he looks, or is he just one of those dogs that hang around tables and are kept merely for show?”

“This hound,” Eumaeus answered, “belonged to the man who died in a distant land. If he were what he was when Odysseus left for Troy, he would soon show you what he could do. There wasn’t a wild beast in the forest that could escape him once he picked up its trail. But now he’s fallen on hard times, since his master is dead and gone, and the women don’t care for him. Servants never do their work properly when their master’s hand is no longer over them—Zeus takes half the goodness out of a man when he makes him a slave.”
As he spoke, he went inside the buildings to the gallery where the suitors were, but Argos died as soon as he had recognized his master.

Telemachus saw Eumaeus long before anyone else did and beckoned him to come sit beside him. The swineherd looked around, picked up a seat that was lying near where the carver sat distributing portions to the suitors, brought it to Telemachus’s table, and sat down across from him. Then the servant brought him his portion and gave him bread from the basket.

Immediately afterward, Odysseus came inside, looking like a poor, miserable old beggar, leaning on his staff with his clothes all in rags. He sat down on the ash-wood threshold just inside the doors leading from the outer to the inner court, against a cypress-wood pillar that the carpenter had skillfully planed and fitted true with rule and line. Telemachus took a whole loaf from the bread basket, along with as much meat as he could hold in both hands, and said to Eumaeus, “Take this to the stranger and tell him to go around to all the suitors and beg from them—a beggar shouldn’t be ashamed.”
So Eumaeus went up to him and said, “Stranger, Telemachus sends you this and says you should go around begging from the suitors, since beggars shouldn’t be ashamed.”
Odysseus answered, “May King Zeus grant Telemachus all happiness and fulfill his heart’s desire.”

Then with both hands he took what Telemachus had sent him and laid it on the filthy old bag at his feet. He continued eating while the bard was singing, and had just finished his meal when the song ended. The suitors applauded the bard. At that Athena came to Odysseus and urged him to beg pieces of bread from each of the suitors, so he could see what kind of people they were and distinguish the good from the bad—though she wasn’t going to save a single one of them regardless. So Odysseus made his rounds, going from left to right, stretching out his hands to beg as if he were a real beggar. Some of them pitied him and were curious about him, asking each other who he was and where he came from. At that the goatherd Melanthius said, “Suitors of my noble mistress, I can tell you something about him, since I’ve seen him before. The swineherd brought him here, but I know nothing about the man himself or where he comes from.”

At this Antinous began abusing the swineherd. “You precious idiot,” he shouted, “what did you bring this man to town for? Don’t we have enough tramps and beggars already to pester us while we eat? Do you think it’s nothing that such people gather here to waste your master’s property—and you had to bring this one too?”

Eumaeus answered, “Antinous, your birth is good, but your words are evil. It wasn’t my idea to bring him here. Who would invite a stranger from a foreign country unless he’s someone who can do public service—a seer, a healer of hurts, a carpenter, or a bard who can charm us with his singing? Such men are welcome everywhere, but no one invites a beggar who will only be a nuisance. You’re always harder on Odysseus’s servants than any of the other suitors, especially on me, but I don’t care as long as Telemachus and Penelope are alive and here.”
But Telemachus said, “Quiet, don’t answer him. Antinous has the bitterest tongue of all the suitors, and he makes the others worse.”

Then turning to Antinous he said, “Antinous, you look after my interests as if I were your son. Why do you want this stranger thrown out of the house? Heaven forbid! Take something and give it to him yourself—I don’t begrudge it, I bid you take it. Never mind my mother or any of the other servants in the house. But I know you won’t do what I say, because you prefer eating things yourself to giving them to others.”
“What do you mean, Telemachus,” Antinous replied, “with this arrogant talk? If all the suitors gave him as much as I will, he wouldn’t come here again for another three months.”

As he spoke, he lifted the footstool that supported his delicate feet from under the table and made as if to throw it at Odysseus. But the other suitors all gave him something and filled his bag with bread and meat. He was about to return to the threshold and eat what the suitors had given him, but first he went up to Antinous and said:

“Sir, give me something. You’re surely not the poorest man here—you look like a chief, the foremost among them all, so you should be a better giver, and I’ll spread word of your generosity far and wide. I too was once a wealthy man with a fine house of my own. In those days I gave to many a tramp like I am now, no matter who he was or what he needed. I had countless servants and all the other things people have who live well and are thought wealthy. But it pleased Zeus to take it all away from me. He sent me with a band of roving robbers to Egypt—it was a long voyage that ruined me. I stationed my ships in the river Aegyptus and ordered my men to stay with them and keep guard while I sent out scouts to survey from every vantage point.

“But the men disobeyed my orders, followed their own impulses, and ravaged the land of the Egyptians, killing the men and taking their wives and children captive. The alarm quickly reached the city, and when they heard the war cry, people came out at daybreak until the plain was filled with soldiers, cavalry and infantry, and with the gleam of armor. Then Zeus spread panic among my men, and they would no longer face the enemy, finding themselves surrounded. The Egyptians killed many of us and took the rest alive for forced labor. As for me, they gave me to a friend they met, to take to Cyprus—a man named Dmetor, son of Iasus, who was a great man in Cyprus. From there I’ve come here in great misery.”

Then Antinous said, “What god can have sent such a pestilence to plague us during our dinner? Get out, into the open part of the court, or I’ll give you Egypt and Cyprus all over again for your insolence and pestering. You’ve begged from everyone else, and they’ve given you plenty, since they have abundance around them and it’s easy to be generous with other people’s property when there’s plenty of it.”

At this Odysseus began to move away, saying, “Your looks, my fine sir, are better than your manners. If you were in your own house, you wouldn’t give a poor man even a pinch of salt, yet here you are in another man’s house, surrounded by abundance, and you can’t find it in yourself to give him even a piece of bread.”

This made Antinous furious, and he glared at him, saying, “You’ll pay for this before you get out of the court.” With these words he hurled a footstool at him, hitting him on the right shoulder blade near the top of his back. Odysseus stood firm as a rock—the blow didn’t even stagger him, but he shook his head silently as he brooded on his revenge. Then he went back to the threshold and sat down, setting his well-filled bag at his feet.

“Listen to me,” he called out, “you suitors of Queen Penelope, so I can speak my mind. A man feels no pain or ache when he’s hit while fighting for his money, his sheep, or his cattle. So too Antinous has struck me while I serve my wretched belly, which always gets people into trouble. Still, if the poor have gods and avenging spirits at all, I pray that Antinous meets a bad end before his wedding day.”
“Sit there and eat your food in silence, or get out,” Antinous shouted. “If you say another word, I’ll have you dragged hand and foot through the courts, and the servants shall flay you alive.”

The other suitors were very displeased at this, and one of the young men said, “Antinous, you did wrong in striking that poor wretch of a tramp. It will be worse for you if he turns out to be some god—we know the gods disguise themselves in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries and travel around the world to see who acts wrongly and who righteously.”

So the suitors spoke, but Antinous paid them no attention. Meanwhile Telemachus was furious about the blow struck against his father, and though no tear fell from his eyes, he shook his head in silence and brooded on his revenge.

When Penelope heard that the beggar had been struck in the banqueting-gallery, she said to her maids, “May Apollo strike you the same way, Antinous,” and her waiting woman Eurynome answered, “If our prayers were answered, not one of the suitors would ever see another sunrise.” Then Penelope said, “Nurse, I hate every single one of them because they mean nothing but harm, but I hate Antinous like the darkness of death itself. A poor unfortunate tramp came begging around the house from sheer need. Everyone else gave him something for his bag, but Antinous hit him on the right shoulder blade with a footstool.”

So she talked with her maids as she sat in her room, while Odysseus was eating his meal. Then she called for the swineherd and said, “Eumaeus, go and tell the stranger to come here. I want to see him and ask him some questions. He seems to have traveled widely, and he might have seen or heard something of my unfortunate husband.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “If only these Achaeans would keep quiet, madam, you would be enchanted by the story of his adventures. I had him three days and three nights in my hut, which was the first place he reached after escaping from his ship, and he still hasn’t finished telling the story of his misfortunes. If he had been the most divinely inspired minstrel in the world, on whose lips all listeners hang spellbound, I couldn’t have been more charmed as I sat in my hut listening to him. He says there’s an old friendship between his house and that of Odysseus, and that he comes from Crete where the descendants of Minos live, after being driven here and there by every kind of misfortune. He also claims that he’s heard Odysseus is alive and nearby among the Thesprotians, and that he’s bringing great wealth home.”

“Call him here then,” said Penelope, “so I too can hear his story. As for the suitors, let them enjoy themselves indoors or out as they please—they have nothing to worry about. Their grain and wine remain untouched in their houses with only servants to consume them, while they keep hanging around our house day after day, sacrificing our oxen, sheep, and fat goats for their feasts, never giving a thought to how much wine they drink. No estate can survive such recklessness, since we no longer have Odysseus to protect us. If he were to return, he and his son would quickly have their revenge.”

As she spoke, Telemachus sneezed so loudly that the whole house echoed with it. Penelope laughed when she heard this and said to Eumaeus, “Go and call the stranger—didn’t you hear how my son sneezed just as I was speaking? This can only mean that all the suitors are going to die, and not one of them will escape. Furthermore, I tell you this and take it to heart: if I’m satisfied that the stranger is telling the truth, I’ll give him a shirt and cloak of good quality.”

When Eumaeus heard this, he went straight to Odysseus and said, “Father stranger, my mistress Penelope, mother of Telemachus, has sent for you. She’s in great sorrow, but she wants to hear anything you can tell her about her husband. If she’s satisfied that you’re telling the truth, she’ll give you a shirt and cloak, which are exactly what you need most. As for food, you can get enough to fill your belly by begging around town from those who are willing to give.”

“I will tell Penelope,” Odysseus answered, “nothing but the absolute truth. I know all about her husband and have shared his sufferings, but I’m afraid of passing through this crowd of cruel suitors—their pride and insolence reach heaven. Just now, as I was going around the house doing no harm, a man struck me painfully, but neither Telemachus nor anyone else defended me. Tell Penelope, therefore, to be patient and wait until sunset. Let her give me a seat close to the fire, since my clothes are very thin—you know they are, as you’ve seen them ever since I first asked for your help—and then she can ask me about her husband’s return.”

The swineherd went back when he heard this, and Penelope said as she saw him cross the threshold, “Why don’t you bring him, Eumaeus? Is he afraid someone will mistreat him, or is he simply shy about coming inside the house? Beggars shouldn’t be ashamed.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “The stranger is being quite reasonable. He’s avoiding the suitors, and he’s only doing what anyone else would do. He asks you to wait until sunset, and it would be much better, madam, for you to have him all to yourself when you can hear him and talk to him as you wish.”
“The man is no fool,” Penelope replied. “It would very likely be as he says, for there are no more abominable people in the whole world than these men.”

When she finished speaking, Eumaeus went back to the suitors, for he had explained everything. Then he went up to Telemachus and said quietly in his ear so no one could overhear, “My dear sir, I’ll now go back to the pigs to look after your property and my own business. You’ll watch what’s happening here, but above all be careful to stay out of danger, for there are many who wish you ill. May Zeus bring them to a bad end before they do us harm.”
“Very well,” Telemachus replied. “Go home after you’ve eaten, and in the morning come here with the animals we’re to sacrifice for the day. Leave the rest to heaven and me.”

At this Eumaeus took his seat again, and when he had finished his dinner, he left the courts and the gallery with the men at table and went back to his pigs. As for the suitors, they soon began amusing themselves with singing and dancing, for evening was now approaching.
